claims.text: The as-manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a homogeneous FCC matrix.
The as-manufactured alloy has a uniform elemental distribution.
The as-manufactured alloy has no pre-existing oxide scale.
Elevated-temperature degradation is governed by the formation and subsequent breakdown of a protective oxide scale.
The governing oxide forms primarily along grain boundaries.
In oxidizing atmospheres, Al and Cr preferentially oxidize at grain boundaries and produce an Al/Cr-rich oxide scale.
The initially formed Al/Cr-rich oxide scale temporarily retards further oxidation.
Thermal stresses and oxide-scale brittleness eventually cause the protective scale to crack or spall.
Scale cracking or spallation locally exposes the alloy substrate.
Local substrate exposure causes embrittlement and rapid crack propagation.
Rapid crack propagation following oxide-scale failure can produce catastrophic failure.
A reducing atmosphere suppresses formation of a coherent oxide scale.
Suppression of the coherent scale in reducing environments permits diffuse internal oxidation.
Diffuse internal oxidation in reducing environments causes gradual embrittlement rather than abrupt catastrophic failure.
Oxidizing exposure will produce initially stable oxidation resistance followed by a sudden loss of mechanical performance and catastrophic intergranular cracking.
Reducing exposure will produce a slower decline in mechanical properties without a sudden failure event.
The as-manufactured alloy has good initial oxidation resistance and mechanical integrity in inert or near-neutral atmospheres.
The proposed mechanism applies over approximately 650–900 °C under distinctly oxidizing or reducing gas compositions.
The timing and magnitude of degradation may depend on processing-related microstructural variations.
The hypothesis is falsified if changing oxygen partial pressure produces no association between oxide-scale integrity or suppression and the corresponding mechanical degradation behavior.
